name: Clause Extraction and Obligation Analysis
title: Clause Extraction and Obligation Analysis
answer: Clause extraction and obligation analysis is the part of contract work that turns an executed or draft agreement into a structured list of who must do what, by when, and on what condition. It covers identifying clause types such as termination, indemnity, payment terms, confidentiality and renewal, then pulling out the parties, dates, thresholds and triggers attached to each. In practice it sits between review and management: the output feeds obligation tracking, risk registers, renewal calendars and downstream drafting. It is not the same as summarising a contract, because the goal is a machine-readable record rather than prose.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Clause extraction and obligation analysis is the part of contract work that turns an executed or draft agreement into a structured list of who must do what, by when, and on what condition. It covers identifying clause types such as termination, indemnity, payment terms, confidentiality and renewal, then pulling out the parties, dates, thresholds and triggers attached to each. In practice it sits between review and management: the output feeds obligation tracking, risk registers, renewal calendars and downstream drafting. It is not the same as summarising a contract, because the goal is a machine-readable record rather than prose.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the contract text itself, usually as PDF or DOCX, plus any amendments, order forms and incorporated exhibits that change the meaning of the main body. Teams typically store documents in a contract lifecycle management system or a document repository, and extraction tools read from there through an API or a batch upload. Language models do the heavy lifting, often paired with rules, regular expressions or a retrieval layer that points the model at the relevant section rather than the whole file. Output lands in a database, spreadsheet or CLM record where each obligation carries its source clause and page reference.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common pattern is to split the document into sections, classify each section by clause type, then extract the specific fields that matter for that type, such as notice period, governing law, liability cap or payment window. Extraction is usually followed by a verification step, either a human reviewer confirming each field against the highlighted source text or a second pass that checks the extracted value against the clause it came from. Obligation analysis adds structure on top: who owes the duty, what action satisfies it, the deadline or trigger, and any condition that suspends or accelerates it. Accuracy is measured against a labelled set of contracts, and the hard cases tend to be defined terms, cross-references, tables and clauses that change meaning when read with an amendment.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Contracts carry confidential commercial terms, personal data and sometimes privileged material, so extraction pipelines need access control, encryption and a clear record of where documents are processed and stored. Provenance matters as much as accuracy: each extracted obligation should point back to the exact clause and version it came from, so a reviewer can check it and so later changes can be traced. Privilege and waiver questions arise when outside counsel or a vendor touches the documents, and retention rules differ by jurisdiction and by the type of agreement. Errors here have real consequences, a missed renewal notice or a misread indemnity can cost money, so the usual practice is to treat extracted output as a draft for human confirmation rather than a final record. This is a description of common practice, not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is from isolated extraction toward obligations that stay live: linked to calendars, approval workflows and amendment history so a change in one clause updates everything downstream. Evaluation is shifting from field-level accuracy on a static test set toward whether the extracted obligation actually matches what the contract requires in context, including cross-references and defined terms. Expect more work on multilingual and non-standard contracts, on explaining why a value was extracted, and on keeping a defensible audit trail. The human role is likely to remain at the confirmation and exception stage, with routine clauses handled automatically and unusual ones escalated.
